steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an HCI paper about CoQuest, our LLM-based agent system that co-creates research questions with researchers. Motivate why research question development needs support, position it within human-AI co-creation work, briefly describe the system and how we studied it, and end with our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Coming up with research questions (RQs) is a critical step in scientific research and discovery. To come up with research ideas that are creative and valuable, researchers usually start by searching the relevant literature and scoping it, and this is especially the case when the search covers works from multiple domains. Developing research questions is also an iterative process. Researchers first have an initial idea or topic in mind, then they search the literature to refine the idea, and they repeat this until they have a research idea they are satisfied with. Reading a lot of literature, synthesizing it and identifying the relevant work can take a lot of time.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are developing rapidly, and scholars have looked into using LLMs to support the process of research literature discovery, which helps users speed up the literature discovery process significantly. Generative AI technologies are also being used widely in many fields to promote creativity. For example, a recent study found that more than 4.9% of users used ChatGPT to support creative ideation. Recent research has shown that smaller language models can be used to generate novel RQs, but there is still a lack of empirical understanding of how humans evaluate RQs that are generated by AI. LLMs are known to have problems with hallucination and lack of factual accuracy, so creating high-quality RQs needs input from human researchers because of their unique backgrounds and expertise. Letting humans and AI co-create novel research questions is especially promising for doing interdisciplinary research.

- Human-AI co-creation and mixed-initiative systems
  - mixed-initiative systems: human users and computer systems contribute to a shared goal
  - design guidelines for human-AI co-creation systems
  - e.g. prior work: should initiative exchange be parallel or turn-taking?
  - gap: influence of AI-driven initiatives/creativity on user experience - perception of creative process, trust in AI, sense of control
  - impact on co-creation results (quality of generated content) not investigated
- CoQuest and how we studied it
  - AI agent initiates RQ generation with LLMs, takes human feedback -> co-creation
  - three panels: RQ Flow Editor (RQ generation), Paper Graph Visualizer (literature space), AI Thoughts (AI's rationales)
  - formative study: four researchers verbalize expected RQ-generation process with AI support -> initial mental model
  - within-subject experiment, 20 participants, HCI researchers
- Contributions
  - theoretical: new mental model for human-AI co-creation of RQs in HCI
  - new agent LLM system, two interaction designs: breadth-first and depth-first (different AI initiative)
  - empirical: AI initiative vs. perceived experience and outcomes; breadth-first -> users 'feel' more creative, more trust (varies by research background); depth-first RQs rated more creative individually
  - co-creation behavior; design implication: intentionally 'slowing down AI', wait times to explore; stronger sense of control
  - ethical implications and concerns; augment creativity, support ideation/scaffolding, not automate HCI research

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Coming up with research questions (RQs) is a critical step in scientific research and discovery. To come up with research ideas that are creative and valuable, researchers usually start by searching the relevant literature and scoping it, and this is especially the case when the search covers works from multiple domains. Developing research questions is also an iterative process. Researchers first have an initial idea or topic in mind, then they search the literature to refine the idea, and they repeat this until they have a research idea they are satisfied with. Reading a lot of literature, synthesizing it and identifying the relevant work can take a lot of time.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are developing rapidly, and scholars have looked into using LLMs to support the process of research literature discovery, which helps users speed up the literature discovery process significantly. Generative AI technologies are also being used widely in many fields to promote creativity. For example, a recent study found that more than 4.9% of users used ChatGPT to support creative ideation. Recent research has shown that smaller language models can be used to generate novel RQs, but there is still a lack of empirical understanding of how humans evaluate RQs that are generated by AI. LLMs are known to have problems with hallucination and lack of factual accuracy, so creating high-quality RQs needs input from human researchers because of their unique backgrounds and expertise. Letting humans and AI co-create novel research questions is especially promising for doing interdisciplinary research.

The idea of human-AI co-creation draws on pioneering research on mixed-initiative systems, where human users and computer systems both contribute to a shared goal. Recent academic work has also introduced a number of design guidelines for human-AI co-creation systems, and these further inspire the design considerations of mixed-initiative systems. For instance, prior work explored whether the exchange of initiatives between humans and AI should be parallel or turn-taking. But there is still a gap in empirical research about how AI-driven initiatives or creativity influence user experiences, such as how users perceive the creative process, their trust in the AI, and their sense of control. Also, how these factors could impact the results of human-AI co-creation, like the quality of the generated content, has not been investigated yet.

So we proposed a new system called CoQuest. It lets an AI agent initiate RQ generation using the power of LLMs and takes humans' feedback into a co-creation process. The system has three panels: the RQ Flow Editor which supports RQ generation, the Paper Graph Visualizer for exploring the literature space, and AI Thoughts which explains the AI's rationales. The system design was informed by a formative study where we invited four researchers to verbalize how they expected the RQ-generation process to go with AI support. The formative study gave us an initial mental model of human-AI co-creation for RQs. We then evaluated the system design with 20 participants who are HCI researchers in a within-subject experiment.

Our work makes the following contributions. First, we propose and evaluate a new mental model for human-AI co-creation of research questions in the HCI research domain, which is a theoretical contribution. Second, we proposed a new agent LLM system and implemented two interaction designs, breadth-first and depth-first, in which the AI agent takes different levels of initiative in helping users develop RQs. Third, we did a within-subject experiment with HCI researchers and got new empirical understandings of how the different initiatives of the AI impact users' perceived experiences and outcomes. Specifically, for the overall experience, the breadth-first design made users "feel" more creative and users trusted it more, though this effect varies by the users' research background; but when users rated individual RQs, they gave the depth-first questions higher creativity scores. Fourth, by observing closely how participants interacted with the AI, we discovered important co-creation behavior and we propose a new design implication, which is to intentionally "slow down AI" and give users wait times to explore the co-creation space. This especially helps users to gain a stronger sense of control. Finally, we discuss what our study implies for designing ethical human-AI co-creation systems, and the potential ethical concerns. We advocate using LLM-based systems to augment human creativity and support the ideation and scaffolding process, rather than using ideas generated by LLMs to automate HCI research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Identifying research questions (RQs) is a critical step of scientific research and discovery [1]. To formulate creative and valuable research ideas, researchers often start by searching and scoping the relevant literature, especially when the search involves works spanning multiple domains [2]. Developing research questions is also iterative: researchers first have an initial idea or topic in mind, then conduct a literature search to refine the idea, and repeat this process until they have a satisfying research idea [3]. Reading a large body of literature, synthesizing it, and identifying the relevant work can be rather time-consuming.

With the rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs), scholars have investigated the potential of using LLMs to support the process of research literature discovery [4,5,6], which helps users significantly speed up literature discovery. Meanwhile, generative AI technologies have also been widely used in various fields to promote creativity [7,8,9]. For example, a recent study found that more than 4.9% of users used ChatGPT to support creative ideation [10]. Although recent research has demonstrated the potential of using smaller language models to generate novel RQs [11], there is still a lack of empirical understanding of how humans evaluate AI-generated RQs. Given that LLMs are known to have problems with hallucination and lack of factual accuracy [12], creating high-quality RQs requires input from human researchers, with their unique backgrounds and expertise. Enabling humans and AI to co-create novel research questions is particularly promising for conducting interdisciplinary research.

The concept of human-AI co-creation draws on pioneering research on mixed-initiative systems, where human users and computer systems contribute to a shared goal [13,14]. Recent academic work has also introduced a variety of design guidelines for human-AI co-creation systems [15,16,17], further inspiring the design considerations of mixed-initiative systems. For instance, [15] explored whether the exchange of initiatives between humans and AI should be designed as parallel or turn-taking. However, there remains a gap in empirical research on how AI-driven initiatives or creativity influence user experiences, such as users' perception of the creative process, trust in the AI, and sense of control. Moreover, the potential impact of these factors on the results of human-AI co-creation, such as the quality of generated content, has yet to be investigated.

To this end, we proposed a novel system called CoQuest, which allows an AI agent to initiate RQ generation using the power of LLMs and takes humans' feedback into a co-creation process. The system consists of three panels: RQ Flow Editor for supporting RQ generation, Paper Graph Visualizer for exploring the literature space, and AI Thoughts for explaining the AI's rationales. The system design was informed by a formative study in which we invited four researchers to verbalize their expected RQ-generation processes with AI support. The formative study yielded an initial mental model of human-AI co-creation for RQs. The system design was then evaluated with 20 participants who are HCI researchers through a within-subject experiment.

Our work makes novel and significant contributions as follows. First, we make a theoretical contribution by proposing and evaluating a new mental model for human-AI co-creation of research questions in the HCI research domain. Second, we proposed a new agent LLM system and implemented two interaction designs (breadth-first and depth-first), in which the AI agent takes different levels of initiative in supporting users to develop RQs. Third, through a within-subject experiment with HCI researchers, we gained new empirical understandings of how the AI's different initiatives impact users' perceived experiences and outcomes. Specifically, for the overall experience, the breadth-first design made users "feel" more creative and gained more trust from users, though the effect varies by users' research background; but when rating individual RQs, users scored the depth-first questions higher for creativity. Fourth, by closely observing participants' interaction with the AI, we discovered important co-creation behavior and proposed a new design implication, namely intentionally "slowing down AI" and giving users wait times to explore the co-creation space. This is especially beneficial for users to gain a stronger sense of control. Finally, we discuss the implications of our study for designing ethical human-AI co-creation systems, along with potential ethical concerns. We advocate employing LLM-based systems to augment human creativity and support the ideation and scaffolding process, rather than using LLM-generated ideas to automate HCI research.
